title: Why God Waited Four Days for Lazarus
paragraphs:
Why God Waited Four Days for Lazarus
The Delay That Felt Like Abandonment Became the Miracle That Changed Everything
Have you ever prayed with all your heart... and heaven stayed silent?
But long enough for hope to start dying.
Long enough for tears to become exhaustion.
Long enough for you to wonder if God even heard you at all.
That is exactly where the story of Lazarus begins.
It begins with a family that loved Jesus deeply and could not understand why He was not coming.
The Gospel of John tells us:
"Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus." (John 11:5)
"So, when He heard that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was two more days." (John 11:6)
John uses the word ἀγαπάω (agapaō) for Jesus' love—a deep, covenantal, self-giving love.
In other words, Jesus delayed not because He lacked love.
He delayed because He loved them.
Because we often assume God's love means immediate rescue.
But Scripture repeatedly shows something different.
Sometimes God's deepest love appears in the form of a painful delay.
Mary and Martha knew Jesus could heal.
They believed His power was sufficient.
Can you imagine the conversations inside that house?
Can you imagine looking down the road every few minutes hoping to see Him arrive?
Some readers know exactly what that feels like.
But John carefully tells us something important.
When Jesus finally arrived, Lazarus had been dead four days.
Why wait until all hope appeared completely gone?
To understand the answer, we need to understand something from the Jewish culture of that time.
While this was not biblical doctrine, many Jews held a traditional belief that a person's spirit lingered near the body for three days after death before finally departing.
By the fourth day, death was considered unquestionably irreversible.
The body had already begun decomposing.
"Lord, by this time there is a bad odor, for he has been there four days." (John 11:39)
Scripture does not sanitize the moment.
This was not a recently deceased man.
This was not a near-death experience.
This was not someone merely unconscious.
The situation was beyond human repair.
Exactly where God often does His greatest work.
Because Jesus was never trying merely to heal Lazarus.
He was revealing who He truly is.
Standing before a grieving Martha, Jesus makes one of the most powerful declarations in all Scripture:

ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
(Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
"I am the resurrection and the life." (John 11:25)
Resurrection is not merely something Jesus does.
The Son of God stands before the grave.
The shortest verse in the Bible contains one of the deepest revelations of God's heart.
Jesus already knew Lazarus would walk out of that tomb.
He knew the miracle was moments away.
Yet He still entered their pain.
Because God does not stand distant from human suffering.
The cross would prove that forever.
Then came the moment that changed history.
Jesus stood before the tomb and cried out:
A man who had been dead four days walked out alive.
And that is where this story becomes intensely personal.
Many people reading this are standing in front of their own "four-day tomb."
Mary and Martha likely thought the same thing.
But God's delays are not God's denials.
The God who waited four days was not absent.
He was preparing a greater revelation.
Because if Jesus had arrived immediately, He would have been known as a healer.
By arriving after four days, He revealed Himself as Lord over death itself.
The delay became part of the miracle.
The waiting became part of the testimony.
The heartbreak became part of the glory.
Jesus had already explained this earlier:
"This sickness will not end in death. It is for the glory of God." (John 11:4)
The Greek word for glory is:
Meaning splendor, honor, divine majesty revealed.
What looked like disaster was actually becoming a stage upon which God's glory would be displayed.
And perhaps that is exactly what is happening in your story right now.
The chapter that feels abandoned may actually be preparation.
Because Jesus specializes in situations that look impossible.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel itself.
Through His death and resurrection, He called dead sinners into eternal life.
The story of Lazarus is ultimately a preview of something even greater.
It points to Christ's own death.
And the salvation He offers every person willing to trust Him.
This is why our theme is more than a slogan.
If this message stirred something inside you, don't keep it to yourself.
Someone you know is standing in front of a four-day tomb right now.
Someone believes their story is finished.
Not because we are building a platform.
But because together we are advancing Gospel-centered discipleship, biblical truth, and the message of Jesus Christ to people who desperately need hope.
Have you been waiting on God longer than you expected?
The grave thought it had the final chapter, but Jesus was only turning the page.
